words.title: HELLO → KUMUSTA
words.speaker: Kalaw
words.teachText:
Let's start with a simple word you'll use often when meeting someone.
In Ilokano, 'kumusta' means 'hello.'
It is a friendly greeting you can use when you meet someone or begin a conversation.
Listen carefully: kumusta.
Now, try saying 'kumusta' yourself.
words.successText: Kumusta! Nailed it! That's a great way to greet someone!

words.title: HOW ARE YOU? → KUMUSTA KA?
words.speaker: Kalaw
words.teachText:
Once you've greeted someone, you can show more warmth by asking how they are.
In Ilokano, 'kumusta ka?' means 'how are you?'
You can use it when checking on a friend, neighbor, or someone you've just met.
Listen carefully: kumusta ka?
Now, try saying 'kumusta ka?' yourself.
words.successText: Kumusta ka! Ah, see that smile? You're making friends already!

words.title: I'M FINE → NASAYAAT AK
words.speaker: Kalaw
words.teachText:
When someone asks you 'kumusta ka?', you can tell them how you're doing.
In Ilokano, 'nasayaat ak' means 'I'm fine' or 'I'm doing well.'
For example, if someone asks how your journey is going, you can answer: 'Nasayaat ak.'
Listen carefully: nasayaat ak.
Now, try saying 'nasayaat ak' yourself.
words.successText: Nasayaat ak! That's the spirit! Keep that energy up!

words.title: GOOD MORNING → NAIMBAG A BIGAT
words.speaker: Kalaw
words.teachText:
Look at the morning sun shining over the tiled roofs of Calle Crisologo.
In Ilokano, 'naimbag a bigat' means 'good morning.'
You can use it when greeting someone earlier in the day.
For example, you can use it when greeting vendors as they begin their morning.
Listen carefully: naimbag a bigat.
Now, try saying 'naimbag a bigat' yourself.
words.successText:
Naimbag a bigat! You've got the morning greeting down!
Fly over to Vendor Kyros's souvenir stall. He'll teach you how to greet people at other times of the day.

2. VENDOR KYROS — SOUVENIR VENDOR

words.title: GOOD AFTERNOON → NAIMBAG A MALEM
words.speaker: Kyros
words.teachText:
Naimbag nga aldaw, traveler! Kalaw told me a new adventurer was exploring Vigan.
When the morning has passed and the afternoon arrives, Ilocanos can greet someone by saying 'naimbag a malem.'
It means 'good afternoon.'
You can use it when greeting someone during the afternoon.
Listen carefully: naimbag a malem.
Now, try saying 'naimbag a malem' yourself.
words.successText: Naimbag a malem! Welcome to my shop, friend!

words.title: GOOD EVENING → NAIMBAG A RABII
words.speaker: Kyros
words.teachText:
As the sun sets and the streetlamps begin to glow, the greeting changes with the time of day.
In Ilokano, 'naimbag a rabii' means 'good evening.'
Use it when greeting someone in the evening.
Listen carefully: naimbag a rabii.
Now, try saying 'naimbag a rabii' yourself.
words.successText: Naimbag a rabii! Look at your pendant glow!

words.title: GOOD DAY → NAIMBAG NGA ALDAW
words.speaker: Kyros
words.teachText:
Sometimes you want to give someone a general greeting without focusing on morning, afternoon, or evening.
In Ilokano, 'naimbag nga aldaw' means 'good day.'
It is a general greeting that can be used to wish someone a pleasant day.
Listen carefully: naimbag nga aldaw.
Now, try saying 'naimbag nga aldaw' yourself.
words.successText: Naimbag nga aldaw! Hope you enjoy your stroll down Calle Crisologo!

words.title: GOODBYE → AGPAKADA AKON
words.speaker: Kyros
words.teachText:
Every journey eventually continues to another place.
When leaving someone, you can say 'agpakada akon' to say 'goodbye.'
Use it when ending a conversation or parting ways.
Listen carefully: agpakada akon.
Now, try saying 'agpakada akon' yourself.
words.successText:
Agpakada akon! ✨ GREETINGS MILESTONE UNLOCKED! ✨
Go meet Vendor Irah at the weaving loom. She has something important to teach you about showing gratitude.

QUEST 2: GRATITUDE
Words 9–13
3. VENDOR IRAH — INABEL WEAVER

words.title: THANK YOU → AGYAMANAK
words.speaker: Irah
words.teachText:
Clack-clack-clack goes the loom! Welcome, traveler!
When someone helps you, gives you something, or does something kind for you, it is important to show appreciation.
In Ilokano, 'agyamanak' means 'thank you.'
You can use it whenever you want to express gratitude.
Listen carefully: agyamanak.
Now, try saying 'agyamanak' yourself.
words.successText: Agyamanak! Showing gratitude helps keep our community close-knit!

words.title: THANK YOU VERY MUCH → AGYAMANAK UNAY
words.speaker: Irah
words.teachText:
Sometimes a simple thank you isn't enough to express how grateful you feel.
In Ilokano, 'agyamanak unay' means 'thank you very much.'
You can use it when someone does something especially kind or generous for you.
Listen carefully: agyamanak unay.
Now, try saying 'agyamanak unay' yourself.
words.successText: Agyamanak unay! May your journey be smooth and bright!

words.title: THANK YOU FOR YOUR HELP → AGYAMANAK ITI TULONG MO
words.speaker: Irah
words.teachText:
When someone gives you a helping hand, you can thank them specifically for their assistance.
In Ilokano, 'agyamanak iti tulong mo' means 'thank you for your help.'
You can use it when someone helps you complete a task or solve a problem.
Listen carefully: agyamanak iti tulong mo.
Now, try saying 'agyamanak iti tulong mo' yourself.
words.successText: Agyamanak iti tulong mo! We Ilocanos love helping one another!

words.title: I AM SORRY → PAKAWANEN NAK
words.speaker: Irah
words.teachText:
Oops! Be careful around these delicate threads.
If you accidentally bump into someone or make a mistake, you can apologize.
In Ilokano, 'pakawanen nak' means 'I am sorry.'
Use it when you want to apologize for something you've done.
Listen carefully: pakawanen nak.
Now, try saying 'pakawanen nak' yourself.
words.successText:
Pakawanen nak... No harm done!
Pop over to Vendor Jom's empanada stall for the last gratitude phrase!

4. VENDOR JOM — EMPANADA VENDOR

words.title: EXCUSE ME → DISPENSAREN NAK
words.speaker: Jom
words.teachText:
Smell that sizzling longganisa? My counter is getting crowded!
When you need to politely get someone's attention or pass through a crowded space, you can say 'dispensaren nak.'
It means 'excuse me.'
Listen carefully: dispensaren nak.
Now, try saying 'dispensaren nak' yourself.
words.successText:
Dispensaren nak! Sharp manners!
✨ GRATITUDE MILESTONE UNLOCKED! ✨
Stick around for the Response trials!

QUEST 3: RESPONSES
Words 14–18
Words 14–18 — JOM

words.title: YES → WEN
words.speaker: Jom
words.teachText:
Let's practice a simple response.
When someone asks you a question and you want to agree or answer 'yes,' Ilokano uses the word 'wen.'
Listen carefully: wen.
Now, try saying 'wen' yourself.
words.successText: Wen! That's what I like to hear! Sizzling away!

words.title: NO → SAAN
words.speaker: Jom
words.teachText:
Of course, sometimes you need to politely disagree or say 'no.'
In Ilokano, 'saan' means 'no.'
You can use it when you want to give a negative response.
Listen carefully: saan.
Now, try saying 'saan' yourself.
words.successText: Saan! Got it! I'll keep that garlic vinegar ready for another time!

words.title: OKAY → OKAY
words.speaker: Jom
words.teachText:
Sometimes you simply want to show that you agree or understand.
In Ilokano, 'okay' can also be used to say 'okay.'
It is a simple response used to acknowledge something or show agreement.
Listen carefully: okay.
Now, try saying 'okay' yourself.
words.successText: Okay! Easy enough! You're picking this up quickly!

words.title: I UNDERSTAND → MAWATAN KO
words.speaker: Jom
words.teachText:
When someone explains something and you want to tell them that you understand, you can use 'maawatan ko.'
It means 'I understand.'
Listen carefully: maawatan ko.
Now, try saying 'maawatan ko' yourself.
words.successText: Maawatan ko! Excellent! You're understanding more and more!

words.title: I DON'T UNDERSTAND → DIAK MAWATAN
words.speaker: Jom
words.teachText:
If someone says something you don't understand, it's useful to let them know.
In Ilokano, 'diak maawatan' means 'I don't understand.'
You can use it when you need someone to explain something again.
Listen carefully: diak maawatan.
Now, try saying 'diak maawatan' yourself.
words.successText:
Diak maawatan! No worries—learning takes practice!
✨ RESPONSES MILESTONE UNLOCKED! ✨

QUEST 4: IDENTITY
Words 19–22
5. RONNIE — LOCAL RESIDENT

words.title: WHAT IS YOUR NAME? → ANIA TI NAGAN MO
words.speaker: Ronnie
words.teachText:
When meeting someone new, one of the first things you may want to know is their name.
In Ilokano, 'ania ti nagan mo?' means 'what is your name?'
You can use this phrase when introducing yourself to someone or asking for their name.
Listen carefully: ania ti nagan mo?
Now, try saying 'ania ti nagan mo?' yourself.
words.successText: Ania ti nagan mo? That's a great question to ask when meeting someone new!

words.title: MY NAME IS ___ → TI NAGAN KO KET ___
words.speaker: Ronnie
words.teachText:
Now it's your turn to introduce yourself.
In Ilokano, 'ti nagan ko ket...' means 'my name is...'
The words 'ti nagan ko ket' form the fixed part of the phrase. You then add your own name.
For example: 'Ti nagan ko ket Jom.'
Listen carefully: ti nagan ko ket Jom.
Now, try introducing yourself using 'ti nagan ko ket...' and your own name.
words.successText:
Awesome to meet you! You just introduced yourself in Ilokano!
Go meet Sally near the brick arch to complete Level I!

6. SALLY — LOCAL RESIDENT

words.title: WHERE ARE YOU FROM? → TAGA SADINO KA
words.speaker: Sally
words.teachText:
When meeting someone new, you may also want to learn where they come from.
In Ilokano, 'taga sadino ka?' means 'where are you from?'
Use it when asking someone about their hometown or place of origin.
Listen carefully: taga sadino ka?
Now, try saying 'taga sadino ka?' yourself.
words.successText: Taga sadino ka? That's how you ask where someone comes from!

words.title: I AM FROM ___ → TAGA ___ AK
words.speaker: Sally
words.teachText:
Now you can answer that question yourself.
In Ilokano, 'taga ___ ak' means 'I am from ___.'
The phrase 'taga' introduces the place you come from, while the location changes depending on your answer.
For example: 'taga Vigan ak.'
Listen carefully: taga Vigan ak.
Now, try saying 'taga' followed by your hometown.
words.successText:
Excellent! You just told me where you're from!
🏆 LEVEL I: CONVERSATIONAL & SOCIAL COMPLETE! 🏆
You've learned how to greet people, express gratitude, respond to others, and introduce yourself.
Your journey now takes you deeper into everyday communication.
Welcome to Level II: Functional & Navigational!

LEVEL II: FUNCTIONAL & NAVIGATIONAL
QUEST 5: REQUESTS
Words 23–27

words.title: HELP ME → TULONGANNAK
words.speaker: Sally
words.teachText:
If you are in trouble or need assistance, you need a direct way to ask for help.
In Ilokano, 'tulunganak' means 'help me.'
Use it when you urgently need someone to assist you.
Listen carefully: tulunganak.
Now, try saying 'tulunganak' yourself.
words.successText: Tulunganak! Don't worry—you're never alone!

words.title: CAN YOU HELP ME → MABALIN KADI A TULONGANNAK
words.speaker: Sally
words.teachText:
Sometimes you want to ask for help more politely.
In Ilokano, 'mabalin kadi a tulunganak?' means 'can you help me?'
This is useful when politely requesting someone's assistance.
Listen carefully: mabalin kadi a tulunganak?
Now, try saying 'mabalin kadi a tulunganak?' yourself.
words.successText:
Mabalin kadi a tulunganak! Perfect!
Find Tour Guide Lito for the rest of these requests!

7. LITO — TOUR GUIDE

words.title: PLEASE WAIT → URAYENNAK
words.speaker: Lito
words.teachText:
Look out! A horse carriage is passing through!
When you need someone to pause and wait for you, you can say 'urayennak.'
It means 'please wait' or 'wait for me.'
Listen carefully: urayennak.
Now, try saying 'urayennak' yourself.
words.successText: Urayennak! Safety first on these narrow streets!

words.title: GIVE ME ___ → IKANMO MAN ___
words.speaker: Lito
words.teachText:
When asking someone to hand you an object, you can use 'ikanmo man...'
It means 'give me...' and you add the item you want afterward.
For example: 'ikanmo man map' — 'give me the map.'
Listen carefully: ikanmo man map.
Now, try saying 'ikanmo man' followed by an object you want.
words.successText: Ikanmo man! Well done! Here is your map of Vigan!

words.title: CAN I ASK → MABALIN KADI AGSALUDSOD
words.speaker: Lito
words.teachText:
Before asking someone a question, it's polite to ask for permission.
In Ilokano, 'mabalin kadi agsaludsod?' means 'can I ask?'
You can use it before asking someone for information.
Listen carefully: mabalin kadi agsaludsod?
Now, try saying 'mabalin kadi agsaludsod?' yourself.
words.successText:
Mabalin kadi agsaludsod! Ask away!
✨ REQUESTS MILESTONE UNLOCKED! ✨

QUEST 6: DIRECTIONS
Words 28–37

words.title: GO STRAIGHT → AGDIRETSO
words.speaker: Lito
words.teachText:
You're heading toward Plaza Salcedo and don't want to make any turns.
In Ilokano, 'agdiretso' means 'go straight.'
You can use it when giving directions or telling someone to continue forward.
Listen carefully: agdiretso.
Now, try saying 'agdiretso' yourself.
words.successText:
Agdiretso! Straight ahead!
Go find Apo Lakay by the stone well for more pathfinding!

8. APO LAKAY — COMMUNITY ELDER

words.title: TURN LEFT → AGLIKO ITI KANNIGID
words.speaker: Apo Lakay
words.teachText:
To reach the Burnay pottery yard, you need to tell someone which direction to take.
In Ilokano, 'agliko iti kannigid' means 'turn left.'
Use it when directing someone to turn toward the left side.
Listen carefully: agliko iti kannigid.
Now, try saying 'agliko iti kannigid' yourself.
words.successText: Agliko iti kannigid! Turn left—the clay kilns are right there!

words.title: TURN RIGHT → AGLIKO ITI KANNAWAN
words.speaker: Apo Lakay
words.teachText:
If you want someone to take the opposite direction, you can tell them to turn right.
In Ilokano, 'agliko iti kannawan' means 'turn right.'
Listen carefully: agliko iti kannawan.
Now, try saying 'agliko iti kannawan' yourself.
words.successText: Agliko iti kannawan! Turn right at the corner!

words.title: GO UP → UMULI ITI NGATO
words.speaker: Apo Lakay
words.teachText:
To reach the top of the tower and see the province below, you need to tell someone to move upward.
In Ilokano, 'umuli iti ngato' means 'go up.'
Use it when directing someone toward a higher place.
Listen carefully: umuli iti ngato.
Now, try saying 'umuli iti ngato' yourself.
words.successText: Umuli iti ngato! Climb up to the top!

words.title: GO DOWN → BUMABA
words.speaker: Apo Lakay
words.teachText:
After enjoying the view, you'll need to return to the ground.
In Ilokano, 'bumaba' means 'go down.'
Use it when telling someone to move toward a lower place.
Listen carefully: bumaba.
Now, try saying 'bumaba' yourself.
words.successText:
Bumaba! Mind your step!
Go see Tomas at the pottery yard!

9. TOMAS — POTTERY MAKER

words.title: STOP HERE → AGSARDENG DITOY
words.speaker: Tomas
words.teachText:
Welcome to the clay yard!
If you want someone to stop at the place where they are standing, you can say 'agsardeng ditoy.'
It means 'stop here.'
Listen carefully: agsardeng ditoy.
Now, try saying 'agsardeng ditoy' yourself.
words.successText: Agsardeng ditoy! Perfect landing spot!

words.title: COME HERE → UMAY DITOY
words.speaker: Tomas
words.teachText:
Sometimes you need to call someone toward you.
In Ilokano, 'umay ditoy' means 'come here.'
Use it when asking someone to move toward your location.
Listen carefully: umay ditoy.
Now, try saying 'umay ditoy' yourself.
words.successText: Umay ditoy! Come take a look at this pottery!

words.title: GO THERE → MAPAN IDIAY
words.speaker: Tomas
words.teachText:
If you want someone to move toward another location, you can direct them away from where you are.
In Ilokano, 'mapan idiay' means 'go there.'
Listen carefully: mapan idiay.
Now, try saying 'mapan idiay' yourself.
words.successText: Mapan idiay! Cool shade is much safer!

words.title: FOLLOW ME → SUROTENNAK
words.speaker: Tomas
words.teachText:
When you want someone to come along with you, you can tell them to follow.
In Ilokano, 'surotennak' means 'follow me.'
Use it when leading someone to another place.
Listen carefully: surotennak.
Now, try saying 'surotennak' yourself.
words.successText:
Surotennak! Follow me to the jar drying racks!

10. KLARA — ANTIQUE SHOP OWNER

words.title: WAIT HERE → URAY DITOY
words.speaker: Klara
words.teachText:
If you need someone to stay in their current location while you do something else, you can tell them to wait.
In Ilokano, 'uray ditoy' means 'wait here.'
Listen carefully: uray ditoy.
Now, try saying 'uray ditoy' yourself.
words.successText:
Uray ditoy!
✨ DIRECTIONS MILESTONE UNLOCKED! ✨
Talk to me again for the Counting lessons!

QUEST 7: COUNT
Words 38–47
10. KLARA — ANTIQUE SHOP OWNER

words.title: ONE → MAYSA
words.speaker: Klara
words.teachText:
Let's begin counting in Ilokano.
The word 'maysa' means 'one.'
You use it when counting a single person or object.
For example, if you see one chest, you can say 'maysa.'
Listen carefully: maysa.
Now, try saying 'maysa' yourself.
words.successText: Maysa! Just one rare chest!

words.title: TWO → DUA
words.speaker: Klara
words.teachText:
When you count two objects, people, or things, Ilokano uses 'dua.'
It means 'two.'
Listen carefully: dua.
Now, try saying 'dua' yourself.
words.successText: Dua! Two matching chairs!

words.title: THREE → TALLO
words.speaker: Klara
words.teachText:
The next number is 'tallo.'
In Ilokano, 'tallo' means 'three.'
For example, you can use it when counting three objects.
Listen carefully: tallo.
Now, try saying 'tallo' yourself.
words.successText:
Tallo! Three oil lamps!
Head over to Tala the Bagnet seller for more numbers!

11. TALA — BAGNET SELLER

words.title: FOUR → UPPAT
words.speaker: Tala
words.teachText:
Let's keep counting.
In Ilokano, 'uppat' means 'four.'
You can use it when counting four objects, such as four pieces of Bagnet.
Listen carefully: uppat.
Now, try saying 'uppat' yourself.
words.successText: Uppat! Four crispy slabs!

words.title: FIVE → LIMA
words.speaker: Tala
words.teachText:
The next number is 'lima.'
In Ilokano, 'lima' means 'five.'
Listen carefully: lima.
Now, try saying 'lima' yourself.
words.successText: Lima! Five kilos of delicious Bagnet!

words.title: SIX → INNEM
words.speaker: Tala
words.teachText:
In Ilokano, the number 'six' is 'innem.'
Listen carefully: innem.
Now, try saying 'innem' yourself.
words.successText: Innem! Six family recipes!

words.title: SEVEN → PITO
words.speaker: Tala
words.teachText:
The Ilokano word for 'seven' is 'pito.'
Listen carefully: pito.
Now, try saying 'pito' yourself.
words.successText:
Pito! Seven!
Run to Mang Lance the Kalesa driver to finish counting!

12. MANG LANCE — KUTSERO / KALESA DRIVER
Quest Objective
SetObjective_Find Wheel Pin
Intro Script
Whoa, hold on! My carriage wheel pin popped out!
Please find the wheel pin so my horse Barnaby and I can ride safely!
Player finds pin and returns it → Quest Completed

words.title: EIGHT → WALO
words.speaker: Mang Lance
words.teachText:
Whew! Thanks for fixing my wheel!
Let's continue counting.
In Ilokano, 'walo' means 'eight.'
Listen carefully: walo.
Now, try saying 'walo' yourself.
words.successText: Walo! Eight treats for Barnaby!

words.title: NINE → SIAM
words.speaker: Mang Lance
words.teachText:
The next number is 'siam.'
In Ilokano, 'siam' means 'nine.'
Listen carefully: siam.
Now, try saying 'siam' yourself.
words.successText: Siam! Nine! You're almost at the end of the count!

words.title: TEN → SANGAPULO
words.speaker: Mang Lance
words.teachText:
And now, we've reached ten!
In Ilokano, 'sangapulo' means 'ten.'
Listen carefully: sangapulo.
Now, try saying 'sangapulo' yourself.
words.successText:
Sangapulo! You made it to ten!
🏆 LEVEL II: FUNCTIONAL & NAVIGATIONAL COMPLETE! 🏆
You've learned how to ask for help, navigate the streets, give directions, and use numbers in everyday situations.
Now let's explore how Ilokano describes actions, people, and ideas.
Welcome to Level III: Grammatical Foundations!

LEVEL III: GRAMMATICAL FOUNDATIONS
QUEST 8: ACTION VERBS
Words 48–55
13. RAYO — PHOTOGRAPHER

words.title: EAT → MANGAN
words.speaker: Mang Lance
words.teachText:
After all that walking, you'll probably be hungry!
In Ilokano, 'mangan' means 'eat.'
It is an action verb used when talking about the act of eating.
For example, when it's time for lunch, you can say 'mangan.'
Listen carefully: mangan.
Now, try saying 'mangan' yourself.
words.successText:
Mangan! Now you're making me hungry!
Go see Rayo the photographer for more action verbs!

13. RAYO — PHOTOGRAPHER

words.title: DRINK → UMINOM
words.speaker: Rayo
words.teachText:
Click! Great pose!
It's warm today, and you might want something refreshing.
In Ilokano, 'uminom' means 'drink.'
It is an action verb used when talking about drinking something.
Listen carefully: uminom.
Now, try saying 'uminom' yourself.
words.successText: Uminom! Refreshing!

words.title: GO → MAPAN
words.speaker: Rayo
words.teachText:
When you want to talk about moving from one place to another, you can use the verb 'mapan.'
It means 'go.'
For example, if you're heading toward a scenic photo spot, you can say 'mapan.'
Listen carefully: mapan.
Now, try saying 'mapan' yourself.
words.successText: Mapan! Let's head over to the arch!

words.title: COME → UMAY
words.speaker: Rayo
words.teachText:
Now let's learn the opposite direction.
In Ilokano, 'umay' means 'come.'
You can use it when asking someone to move toward you or toward a particular place.
Listen carefully: umay.
Now, try saying 'umay' yourself.
words.successText: Umay! Come stand right by the window!

words.title: SLEEP → MATUROG
words.speaker: Rayo
words.teachText:
After exploring all day, everyone needs time to rest.
In Ilokano, 'maturog' means 'sleep.'
It is the action of resting while asleep.
Listen carefully: maturog.
Now, try saying 'maturog' yourself.
words.successText:
Maturog well!
Catch up with Aling Rosa to wrap up Action Verbs!

14. ALING ROSA — SOUVENIR AUNTIE
Quest Objective
SetObjective_Find Thread
Intro Script
Ay, my thread broke!
Please find some thread so I can finish weaving these colorful souvenirs!
Player finds thread and returns it → Quest Completed

words.title: SEE → MAKITA
words.speaker: Aling Rosa
words.teachText:
Aww, thank you!
When you look at something or notice something with your eyes, the Ilokano verb 'makita' means 'see.'
For example, you can use it when looking at these bright textiles.
Listen carefully: makita.
Now, try saying 'makita' yourself.
words.successText: Makita! Look at these lovely patterns!

words.title: HEAR → MANGNGEG
words.speaker: Aling Rosa
words.teachText:
Listen closely. Can you hear the horse hooves clattering down Calle Crisologo?
In Ilokano, 'mangngeg' means 'hear.'
Listen carefully: mangngeg.
Now, try saying 'mangngeg' yourself.
words.successText: Mangngeg! You can hear the kalesas coming!

words.title: SPEAK → AGSAO
words.speaker: Aling Rosa
words.teachText:
You're doing something very important right now—you are using your voice.
In Ilokano, 'agsao' means 'speak.'
You can use it when talking about speaking with another person or practicing a language.
Listen carefully: agsao.
Now, try saying 'agsao' yourself.
words.successText:
Agsao!
✨ ACTION VERBS MILESTONE UNLOCKED! ✨
Stay here for Linking Verbs!

QUEST 9: LINKING VERBS & CONNECTORS
Words 56–65

words.title: AM / SUBJECT CONNECTOR → KET
words.speaker: Aling Rosa
words.teachText:
Now we're moving into a more advanced part of Ilokano.
In a sentence such as 'Siak ket weaver,' the word 'ket' connects the subject with the information that describes it.
Think of 'ket' as a connector that helps link the two parts of the sentence.
Listen carefully: ket.
Now, try saying 'ket' yourself.
words.successText:
Ket! Spot on!
Go see Lola Nida for more connector words!

15. LOLA NIDA — ELDERLY RESIDENT

words.title: IS / SPECIFIC MARKER → ISU TI
words.speaker: Lola Nida
words.teachText:
When identifying or describing something specific, Ilokano can use 'isu ti' as part of the sentence structure.
For example, it can help express an idea similar to 'is the' in English.
Listen carefully: isu ti.
Now, try saying 'isu ti' yourself.
words.successText: Isu ti! You're learning how Ilokano connects ideas!

words.title: PLURAL SUBJECT MARKER → DA
words.speaker: Lola Nida
words.teachText:
When talking about a group of people, Ilokano can use 'da' as a plural marker.
For example, when referring to a group such as the weavers, 'da' can help indicate that you're talking about more than one person.
Listen carefully: da.
Now, try saying 'da' yourself.
words.successText: Da! You're learning how Ilokano expresses groups!

words.title: WAS / PAST STATE → KET IDI
words.speaker: Lola Nida
words.teachText:
When talking about something that existed or was true in the past, you can use 'ket idi' in a historical context.
For example, when describing how a place was in the past, this phrase can help connect the subject with its former state.
Listen carefully: ket idi.
Now, try saying 'ket idi' yourself.
words.successText: Ket idi! You're connecting language with the history of Ilocos!

words.title: WERE / PLURAL PAST STATE → KET IDI
words.speaker: Lola Nida
words.teachText:
The same past expression can also appear when talking about a group in a historical context.
For example, when describing what people were like in the past, 'ket idi' can be part of the sentence structure.
Listen carefully: ket idi.
Now, try saying 'ket idi' yourself.
words.successText:
Ket idi! The past lives on through the stories we tell!

16. NENENG — STUDENT

words.title: BECOME → AGBALIN
words.speaker: Neneng
words.teachText:
Hey! Here's an interesting one.
In Ilokano, 'agbalin' means 'become.'
It describes a change from one state or condition into another.
For example, with practice, you can become more confident in speaking Ilokano.
Listen carefully: agbalin.
Now, try saying 'agbalin' yourself.
words.successText: Agbalin! With practice, you can become a confident Ilokano speaker!

words.title: SEEM / LIKE → KASLA
words.speaker: Neneng
words.teachText:
Sometimes we want to describe how something appears or feels to us.
In Ilokano, 'kasla' can express the idea of 'seem' or 'like.'
For example, you might say something seems like a journey through time.
Listen carefully: kasla.
Now, try saying 'kasla' yourself.
words.successText: Kasla! It really does feel like traveling back through history!

words.title: REMAIN → AGTALINAED
words.speaker: Neneng
words.teachText:
Some things change, but others continue to stay strong.
In Ilokano, 'agtalinaed' means 'remain.'
You can use it when talking about something continuing to exist or stay in a certain state.
Listen carefully: agtalinaed.
Now, try saying 'agtalinaed' yourself.
words.successText: Agtalinaed! May our culture remain strong for generations!

words.title: STAY / RESIDE → AGYAN
words.speaker: Neneng
words.teachText:
When talking about staying or residing in a place, Ilokano uses 'agyan.'
You can use it when talking about where someone stays or lives.
Listen carefully: agyan.
Now, try saying 'agyan' yourself.
words.successText:
Agyan! I hope you stay in Vigan a little longer!
Go see Aling Riza at the restaurant!

17. ALING RIZA — RESTAURANT OWNER

words.title: FEEL / PERCEIVE → MARIKNA
words.speaker: Aling Riza
words.teachText:
Language is more than words. Sometimes, it is about what you experience.
In Ilokano, 'marikna' means 'feel' or 'perceive.'
You can use it when talking about experiencing something through your senses or emotions.
Listen carefully: marikna.
Now, try saying 'marikna' yourself.
words.successText:
Marikna!

words.title: I → SIAK
words.speaker: Aling Riza
words.teachText:
Let's learn words that help us talk about people.
In Ilokano, 'siak' means 'I.'
You use it when referring to yourself.
Listen carefully: siak.
Now, try saying 'siak' yourself.
words.successText: Siak! That's you!

words.title: YOU → SIKA
words.speaker: Aling Riza
words.teachText:
When speaking directly to another person, Ilokano uses 'sika' for 'you.'
Listen carefully: sika.
Now, try saying 'sika' yourself.
words.successText: Sika! That's the word for the person you're speaking to!

words.title: HE → ISUNA
words.speaker: Aling Riza
words.teachText:
When talking about a male person who is not the speaker or listener, Ilokano uses 'isuna' for 'he.'
Listen carefully: isuna.
Now, try saying 'isuna' yourself.
words.successText: Isuna! You're talking about someone else!

words.title: SHE → ISUNA
words.speaker: Aling Riza
words.teachText:
Interestingly, the same Ilokano pronoun 'isuna' can refer to 'she' as well.
The meaning depends on the person you're talking about and the context.
Listen carefully: isuna.
Now, try saying 'isuna' yourself.
words.successText: Isuna! Context helps us understand who we're talking about!

words.title: WE → DAKKAMI
words.speaker: Aling Riza
words.teachText:
When talking about yourself together with other people, you can use 'dakkami' for 'we' in the context taught here.
Listen carefully: dakkami.
Now, try saying 'dakkami' yourself.
words.successText: Dakkami! Now you're speaking as part of a group!

words.title: THEY → ISUDA
words.speaker: Aling Riza
words.teachText:
When talking about a group of other people, Ilokano uses 'isuda' for 'they.'
Listen carefully: isuda.
Now, try saying 'isuda' yourself.
words.successText: Isuda! You're talking about them!

words.title: ME → SIAK
words.speaker: Aling Riza
words.teachText:
Ilokano can use 'siak' when referring to 'me' as well, depending on the sentence structure.
Listen carefully: siak.
Now, try saying 'siak' yourself.
words.successText: Siak! You're getting comfortable with these pronouns!

words.title: US → DAKKAMI
words.speaker: Aling Riza
words.teachText:
When referring to yourself together with others, 'dakkami' can represent 'us' in the context we're learning.
Listen carefully: dakkami.
Now, try saying 'dakkami' yourself.
words.successText: Dakkami! Language helps us describe who belongs together!

words.title: THEM → ISUDA
words.speaker: Aling Riza
words.teachText:
When referring to other people as the object of an action, 'isuda' is used in the context we're learning for 'them.'
Listen carefully: isuda.
Now, try saying 'isuda' yourself.
words.successText:
Isuda! You've learned how Ilokano can talk about different people!

QUEST 11: INTERROGATIVES

18. LOLA BEBANG — ELDERLY RESIDENT

words.title: WHAT → ANIA
words.speaker: Lola Bebang
words.teachText:
Questions help us learn about the world around us.
In Ilokano, 'ania' means 'what.'
Use it when asking about an object, thing, or information.
Listen carefully: ania.
Now, try saying 'ania' yourself.
words.successText: Ania! You're ready to ask questions!

words.title: WHO → ASINO
words.speaker: Lola Bebang
words.teachText:
When you want to know which person you are talking about, use 'asino.'
It means 'who.'
Listen carefully: asino.
Now, try saying 'asino' yourself.
words.successText: Asino! Now you can ask who someone is!

words.title: WHERE → SADINO
words.speaker: Lola Bebang
words.teachText:
When you need to find a place or location, you can ask 'where?'
In Ilokano, 'sadino' means 'where.'
Listen carefully: sadino.
Now, try saying 'sadino' yourself.
words.successText: Sadino! Now you can ask where something is!

words.title: WHEN → KAANO
words.speaker: Lola Bebang
words.teachText:
When asking about time, you can use 'kaano.'
It means 'when.'
Listen carefully: kaano.
Now, try saying 'kaano' yourself.
words.successText: Kaano! Now you can ask about when something happened!

words.title: WHY → APAY
words.speaker: Lola Bebang
words.teachText:
Sometimes we want to understand the reason behind something.
In Ilokano, 'apay' means 'why.'
Use it when asking for a reason or explanation.
Listen carefully: apay.
Now, try saying 'apay' yourself.
words.successText: Apay! Now you can ask why!

words.title: HOW → KASANO
words.speaker: Lola Bebang
words.teachText:
When you want to ask about the way something is done, use 'kasano.'
It means 'how.'
Listen carefully: kasano.
Now, try saying 'kasano' yourself.
words.successText: Kasano! Look how far you've come!

words.title: HOW MANY → MANO
words.speaker: Lola Bebang
words.teachText:
And now, you've reached another important question.
When you want to ask about quantity, Ilokano uses 'mano' for 'how many.'
You can use it when asking about the number of people or objects.
Listen carefully: mano.
Now, try saying 'mano' yourself.
words.successText:
Mano! Now you can ask about quantity and numbers.
